restaurant_name: Northern Regional Veterinary Healthcare and Learning Center
text:
A cold experience with a lack of humanity. They asked for us to give them our terminal kittens body before we even had the chance to process the news he has 3 months to live.

The vets are fine when it comes to treatment/diagnosis. But communication, in both english and thai are awful and they'll just rack up your bill without any warning.

(Never tick the box that lets a student treat your pet. We took a rescue there once and he told us the cat was very newly pregnant and 3 years old. The cat was 8 months old and gave birth 2 weeks later)

After being told our kitten needs surgery, they asked us to take him home and bring him back the next morning. I asked them how much the surgery would cost, they told it would be 3000-4000 baht.

We explained we won't be able to and it's better if he can stay here for the night. They initially refused, but then agreed once we explained multiple times we are struggling to book a car to bring us.

We then site around for about 30 minutes until a man comes up and just takes our kitten back with no information on what is going on now. They just left us sitting in the lobby.

We looked through to see and saw they started to set him up with an IV when he didn't need one - they had already told us he can go home for the night which means he didn't need an IV, if he needed an IV they would have asked us to keep him. Just a way they can increase your bills.

Had to then wait for 40-45 minutes to eventually be told no more information.

Was then called to the counter where I was then asked to make a deposit of 6000 baht - after being told 3000-4000.

They then explain it has some after care included - fine - so I gave them my card and they charged me 3000 baht. When I said that's 3000 not 6000, they said yes this is for another bill. One they hadn't even shown me yet. They charged my card without evening showing me my bill.

So total was 9000 baht. After I pay the money, they then ask me to go out to a pet shop to buy pee pads for our kitten because they don't have any now. I just gave them 9000 baht and they're asking me to spend more money on the most basic things they should have plenty of.

Next day, they called to explain the situation had changed and no longer having surgery. When I asked what their plan was they only said he would be seeing a cardiologist and we could come visit him at 3pm.

We arrive at 3pm to be told we can't go visit him now and have to wait 10 minutes. Waited 10 minutes to then be told we have to wait another 30 minutes.

Eventually we are allowed to go see him. But he's in a oxygen chamber. I asked before what their plan was and they did not tell me they would be putting him in an expensive oxygen chamber.

They then explained to us the kitten has a rare heart disease and has 3-15 months to live. He will now require us to give him an injection each day and some medicine.

The cardiologist didn't even bother to come speak to us or explain anything.

Before we can even process being told our 13 week kitten is terminal, they are now asking us to give them his body once he dies because they want to inspect it as they are interested. I could not believe this. No empathy at all.

We agree to pick him up later that evening to find out it is actually 2 injections per day and 5 x medicine.

We are expecting to get some deposit back because we paid for surgery and 7 nights, only to find out they spent the difference on a bunch more blood tests that they did not explain or give us any warning to despite us asking them what their plan is with them.

Some of the test they performed we had done previously, we already knew he was FIV and FELV negative, but they do the test because it gets them another 300 baht.

Paid almost 6000 baht for one night. Very convenient how the final bill was almost exactly the same as what they told us the surgery would cost.

I don't understand why they don't just give you estimates or provide information on what they are doing so you can be prepared for the price.

text:
It's extremely difficult to contact the attending vet directly; it's almost impossible. You have to call the central office, and then they'll coordinate.
The cat ward definitely doesn't have anyone watching 24/7. From my experience visiting my cat, the cat ward is very enclosed. You wouldn't know how your cat is unless you went inside. If your cat really needs to be admitted, I'd say move it.

I admitted my cat for just one night. The next morning, the vet informed me that my cat had stopped breathing because a staff member fed it and it choked on food, causing shock and respiratory arrest.
Was there any staff member there? How long did the cat stop breathing? How many minutes later were they seen? The cat certainly didn't vomit immediately after eating. I'm still bothered by this. I'd love to see the CCTV footage, but that's probably difficult. Even the vet is hard to contact. My cat stayed in the intensive care unit for another two days. The cat wasn't doing well, and the attending vet and the intensive care unit vet disagreed on whether to give it anti-seizure medication. The attending vet wanted it, but the intensive care unit vet didn't. In the end, they gave it at 9 PM. The cat received the medication, but it was too late. The cat had already had seizures that morning, and its brain was severely damaged. The treatment process was very slow and unprofessional.
I'm extremely disappointed with this hospital.

My recommendation is: if you bring your dog or cat for symptomatic treatment and don't need admission, I strongly advise against it. I think there are many doctors here, and many specialists.
But the service is very slow. Even though our cat had a slot with a professor doctor, we were still transferred to another doctor. However, the doctor who took over the case
seemed very dedicated to providing care.
But regarding other services, such as boarding, don't transfer your cat to another hospital. At least at other hospitals, you can talk directly to the doctor, request to see CCTV footage, and the boarding area has someone watching 24/7. There aren't as many rules as here.

Our cat stayed at this hospital for 3 days and it cost over 10,000 baht. It's not cheap at all. I recommend going somewhere else based on my honest experience.

restaurant_name: Northern Regional Veterinary Healthcare and Learning Center
text:
My experience at the Northern Regional Veterinary Hospital (NOVEL CMU) at Chiang Mai University was, overall, terrible. Here is my honest account. I typed this entirely by hand and stand by my review. (Giving 3 stars to avoid malicious deletion of my review 🙂)

1. Limited Advantages: Friendly veterinarians, separate outpatient areas for cats and dogs

The hospital is large, with separate outpatient areas for cats and dogs, so they don't disturb each other and are cat-friendly. The veterinarians (randomly assigned) were calm and friendly, and communication was barely smooth. Chinese-speaking staff are available at the front desk. They are nice, but cannot translate some medical terms, so a translator and Google Translate are still needed.

2. Poor Inpatient Services

Let me start with what I found worst. My cat has chronic kidney disease and pancreatitis, and acute attacks require hospitalization. This was his third hospitalization, and the worst one I've experienced.

The inpatient veterinarian: Her English was very poor, making communication difficult. Even using Google Translate to translate into Thai, it was still difficult to communicate with her because she seemed impatient. The staff were incredibly indifferent. When I came to see the cat, it suddenly vomited a large amount of yellow fluid, looking extremely distressed, its tongue unable to retract. The staff member simply placed a pee pad to absorb the fluid, without even glancing at the cat! I'll never forget this detail. After a while, I noticed the cat still couldn't retract its tongue, was breathing rapidly, and its limbs were cold. I ran to their office and asked other veterinarians before they finally called her to examine it. Even then, she seemed reluctant; it was absurd.

The reason it's so difficult to find anyone in this ward is because they refuse to give owners their phone numbers. There's only a bell at the front desk; you press it and someone comes out to talk to you, otherwise, there's nothing you can do. So, in this urgent situation, I had to break the rules and go to their office to find someone.

3. The care in the ward is extremely poor.

The price in the ward is astronomical for Chiang Mai!!! Starting at 1500 baht per night. This price is comparable to Beijing, but the quality of care and communication with owners is absolutely terrible.

Every day when I visit my cat, she has to wear an Elizabethan collar, something I've never experienced before. Because she can't eat with the collar on, and given her illness and loss of appetite, the caregivers force-feed her, resulting in her vomit and vomit piling up inside the collar, which no one cleans up.

When I visit her, she smells terrible, and her chin is wet and yellowish. I always hold back tears and spend a long time cleaning her. This clean-loving cat is so pitiful!!!

I suggested to the vet that they remove her Elizabethan collar, at least when she's eating. Then that vet (the one mentioned above 🙄) tells me, "No, your cat is very aggressive; she'll scratch the vet if she doesn't wear it." I asked her, "You're here to see the cat; she's so sick she's on her deathbed. How can she have the strength to scratch you?!" At that time, my cat was so sick she could barely open her eyes and was constantly drooling, and she, as a veterinarian, completely ignored her condition. It was truly shocking.

Me??? My cat??? My cat is so wronged! After so many hospital visits, the vet only ever said he meows loudly; he never scratches, not even with his claws!

Later, a friend working at Chiang Mai University told me that this hospital has many interns with limited experience. This information is for reference only. 🤷‍♀️

4. Poor Communication

We can communicate via Line and phone, but only with the front desk, who then connects us to a doctor, making the process very slow. They only reply during outpatient hours. In hospitalization cases like this, the owner can't proactively communicate with the hospital, and they don't send any photos or videos of the cat or dog in the hospital. After my cat was discharged, I asked them about medication and other issues, but they completely ignored my messages and didn't reply.

5. Questioning the Doctor

My cat stayed in the hospital for three days. Compared to previous illnesses, I felt this clinic's medication was very traditional and conservative, to the point that after three days, my cat's mental state and appetite (still not eating or drinking) showed no improvement whatsoever. The vomiting persisted after hospitalization and IV fluids, but was not improved by injections or tablets of Ceramide. The inflammation was high, with liver and gallbladder inflammation, but antibiotics were completely avoided, not even basic broad-spectrum antibiotics. It's frustrating; the prescribed medication felt like a punch to cotton.

6. Changing hospitals further solidified my dislike for this one.

Thanks to a friend's recommendation, I decisively switched hospitals and doctors. The new doctor was very gentle and professional, and communication was smooth. I told this doctor that the previous hospital said my cat meowed very loudly, making them afraid of being attacked. This doctor just laughed and said, "Aggressive cats don't meow at all!" To prevent my cat from needing hospitalization and wearing an Elizabethan collar, the doctor patiently and softly cared for her. My cat wasn't at all like the CMU doctor had described, needing four or five doctors to hold her down for injections and meals. Afterwards, my cat was very well-behaved in the arms of any medical staff member!
